stem: Pritchard criteria include all of the following except
options: Ability to follow proceedings in the court
Ability to understand the difference between diminished responsibility vs automatisms
Ability to challenge any of the jurors to whom they might object
correctAnswer: Ability to understand the difference between diminished responsibility vs automatisms
explanation:
R v Pritchard criteria are often cited when discussing the ‘test’ for fitness to plead. An individual is unfit to plead if they are unable to: · Understand the course of proceedings on trial

· To comprehend the details of evidence · To know they might challenge any of the jurors to whom they might object · To instruct legal counsel
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 774.

stem: Which of the following defendants is most likely to be fit to plead in a court trial?
options: A defendant who cannot understand the nature of the charges
A defendant with amnesia for the offence
A defendant who does not understand trial procedures
A defendant with lack of ability to challenge the jurors
A defendant who is catatonic, mute and not able to communicate
correctAnswer: A defendant with amnesia for the offence
explanation:
R v Pritchard criteria are often cited when discussing the ‘test’ for fitness to plead. An individual is unfit to plead if they are unable to:

Understand the course of proceedings on trial

To comprehend the details of evidence To know they might challenge any of the jurors to whom they might object To instruct legal counsel

These factors are relevant at the time of trial only (not for arrest or laying charges). Amnesia for the offence does not interfere with fitness to plead, but short-term memory failure due to organic impairments may be such as to make following proceedings in court impossible.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 774-775.

stem: The prevalence of psychotic disorders in prisons compared to the general population is
explanation:
A rate higher by ten times (in the UK, Ref: Brugha et al., 2005) to twenty times (elsewhere), giving a prevalence rate - 2-15% has been noted in various studies. Fazel and Danesh conducted a meta-analysis of 62 surveys from 12 countries including 22 790 prisoners wherein 3-7% of men had psychotic illnesses, 10% major depression, and 65% a personality disorder, including 47% with antisocial personality disorder. Prisoners were about ten times more likely to have antisocial personality disorder than the general population. Fazel, S and Danesh, J (2002)

Serious mental disorders in 23 000 prisoners: a systematic review of 62 surveys. The Lancet 359, 545-550.

stem: Five patients are being discharged from a psychiatric inpatient unit. Considering their diagnostic profile, choose the one who has the highest risk of being violent in next six months.
options: 33 year old man with bipolar disorder
30 year old man with mixed personality disorder
32 year old man with a substance use disorder
correctAnswer: 32 year old man with a substance use disorder
explanation: Alcohol and drug-related problems are more strongly linked to offending and violence than any other mental disorders. A number of aspects of alcohol and substance misuse may be relevant - direct effects of intoxication or withdrawal; funding the habit; personal and social consequences of dependence; the neuropsychiatric sequelae of prolonged misuse; and the social context (peer group, socio-economic deprivation, childhood mistreatment). Also, personal characteristics (impulsivity and sensation seeking), which may lead to substance misuse, may also be associated with offending.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 747.

stem: When women with psychosis commit homicide, their victims are most often aged
explanation: When women with psychosis kill another person, the victim is most commonly a family member <18 years old. Homicide of a child is more likely to be committed by a male. stem: The proportion of those discharged from medium secure units that are convicted for a violent offence within five years of discharge is
explanation:
Follow-up studies of Medium Secure discharges suggest that nearly 25% will be readmitted within the 12 months after discharge. The reconviction rate for any offence in 2 years is 15%, but for violent offences this is 6%. This rate nearly doubles to 1 in 3 reoffending in 5 years, but only 1 in 6 will be convicted for a violent offence. From high secure units, at least 20% of those discharged will never live in the community in the ten years after discharge: they get re-institutionalised elsewhere. In this time at least 15% would have been convicted for a

serious further offence.

stem: Aversion therapy, as historically used in the treatment of several types of paraphilias, is what kind of treatment?
explanation: Initial treatments addressing paraphilic behaviours were generated in the late 1800s. Both Charcot & Magnan and von Schrenck-Notzing outlined methods for resolving ‘unusual’ sexual interests. However, little was done after these early attempts until a series of single case reports emerged in the 1950s, mostly conducted by staff at the Institute of Psychiatry of the University of London. Psychiatrists at this Institute reported the effectiveness of behavioural conditioning-based treatments (such as electric aversion therapy) for several types of paraphilias. However, it was not long before the limits of these Pavlovian treatment approaches became apparent.
reference: Marshall WL. A brief history of psychological theory, research, and treatment with adult male sex offenders. Current Psychiatry Reports. 2018 Aug;20(8):1-8.

stem: Approximately what percentage of people who commit homicides have a mental illness?
explanation: Homicide is the killing of a person by another. A minority of offenders are mentally disordered. From 1993-2019 there were 1540 cases of people being killed by people with mental health conditions in the UK. 11% of people convicted of homicide in the UK from 2005-2015 were mental health patients, most diagnosed with schizophrenia. On average there are around 120 victims of homicide by patients or people who were mentally ill at the time of offence in the UK every year. Many of the victims are children, many are elderly, and many are patients themselves. Victims of homicides by mentally disordered offenders are more often acquaintances (especially a member of the perpetrator’s family), rather than strangers.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 732-733. https://blogs.bmj.com/bmj/2019/06/28/sarah-markham-we-have-to-learn-from-homicides-committed-by-mental-health-patients

Being a member of a minority ethnic group
explanation: Prison suicide and self-harm has been rising in the UK. The most common method of suicide in prison is hanging. The majority of suicides occur within 6 months of imprisonment; life-sentence prisoners are over-represented. Occupying a single cell/solitary confinement is a particularly strong risk factor for both self-harm and suicide. Remand prisoners, young offenders, and those with a history of substance misuse and violent offences are also at higher risk of suicide.

explanation: Arson is a criminal act in which one willfully and maliciously sets fire to or aids in setting fire to a structure, dwelling, or property of another. Most arsonists are male, aged late adolescence-early adulthood, unmarried, poorly educated, living alone, and unemployed or unskilled labourers. Psychiatric disorders are over-represented in arsonists compared to the general population and other offender groups. Substance use disorders (especially alcohol) and personality disorders (particularly antisocial) are most common. Others include psychotic disorders and intellectual disability/low intellectual functioning.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is repeatedly charged with shoplifting and is subsequently diagnosed with kleptomania. Kleptomania is classified as which of the following in ICD-11?
explanation: In ICD-11, kleptomania is classified as an impulse control disorder. Kleptomania is characterised by a recurrent failure to control strong impulses to steal objects in the absence of an apparent motive (e.g., objects are not acquired for personal use or monetary gain). There is an increasing sense of tension or affective arousal before instances of theft and a sense of pleasure, excitement, relief, or gratification during and immediately after the act of stealing. After stealing items, many individuals with kleptomania experience guilt or shame for having committed a theft, but these feelings do not prevent recurrence of the behaviour. Women are significantly more likely to be diagnosed with kleptomania than men.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: Which of the following is true concerning paraphilic disorders?
options: Isolated paraphilic disorders warrant detention under the Mental Health Act 1983
They involve persistent, intense patterns of atypical sexual arousal
They are more common in women than men
They are defined in ICD-11, but not DSM-5
They are never associated with dangerous behaviours
correctAnswer: They involve persistent, intense patterns of atypical sexual arousal
explanation: Paraphilic disorders are characterised by persistent and intense patterns of atypical sexual arousal, manifested by sexual thoughts, fantasies, urges, or behaviours, the focus of which involves others whose age or status renders them unwilling or unable to consent and on which the person has acted or by which he or she is markedly distressed. They are defined in both DSM-5 and ICD-11. Paraphilic disorders are more common in males than females. There is overlap between these disorders, sex offending, and inappropriate sexual behaviour.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020) Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 504-505.

stem: A death resulting from intentional act to kill, but because of provocation, is termed
explanation: Manslaughter/culpable homicide may be voluntary or involuntary. Voluntary culpable homicide is defined as killing with intent to murder, but a partial defence applies (e.g. suicide pact, severe provocation). Involuntary culpable homicide applies when the conduct was grossly negligent, given the risk of death, and did kill; or when the conduct was an unlawful act involving a danger of harm and resulted in death.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 732.

stem: Which of the following syndromes is associated with military prisoners?
explanation: In 1898, Ganser described four criminals showing several common features, including clouding of consciousness with disorientation, auditory and visual hallucinations (or pseudo-hallucinations), amnesia for the period during which the symptoms manifest, conversion symptoms and recent head injury, infection, and severe emotional stress. Approximate answers suggest that the patient understands questions but appears to be deliberately avoiding the correct answer. Ganser believed this to be a hysterical condition with the unconscious production of symptoms to avoid a court appearance. Many now believe that Ganser syndrome is indicative of either an organic or a psychotic state, rather than hysteria as originally believed. A similar condition of approximate answers is found in those consciously feigning illness - this should be called malingering or factitious disorder according to the nature of the gain. Ganser syndrome and malingering/factitious disorder are often confused despite the conscious basis for the latter.
reference: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. pp. 68-69.

explanation: In ICD-11, conduct-dissocial disorder is characterised by a repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms, rules, or laws are violated such as aggression towards people or animals; destruction of property; deceitfulness or theft; and serious violations of rules. Deceitfulness or theft may include stealing items of value (e.g., shoplifting, forgery), lying to obtain goods or favours or to avoid obligations, and/or breaking into someone’s house, building, or car.

stem: Insane automatisms due to sleepwalking may be offered as a defence in court. Which of the following features makes a diagnosis of sleepwalking more likely?
options: Offence occurs within 2 hours of going to sleep
Awakening with intense feelings of anxiety and fear
Attempts are made to conceal the offence
correctAnswer: Offence occurs within 2 hours of going to sleep
explanation: If an individual commits an offence when their body is not under the control of their mind, (e.g. when asleep), they are not guilty of the offence. Legally, this is called an automatism. Insane automatisms are due to an intrinsic cause (e.g. sleepwalking, brain tumours, epilepsy) and result in acquittal on the grounds of insanity. Sleepwalking involves complex, automatic behaviours (automatisms) such as wandering, attempting to dress or undress, carrying objects, eating, urinating in unusual places, and rarely driving a car or sexual behaviour. Behaviours usually occur 15-120 minutes following sleep onset. The activity never appears intentional or planned, and only rarely does aggressive behaviour occur. The person usually has no recollection of the episode. If awakened during the episode, they are usually confused and disoriented.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 460, 778.

stem: Which of the following is classified under sane automatism?
explanation: If an individual commits an offence when their body is not under the control of their mind, (e.g. when asleep), they are not guilty of the offence. Legally, this is called an automatism. In England and Wales, two legal types of automatism are recognised: insane and sane (automatism simpliciter). The distinction is based on whether the behaviour is likely to recur. Insane automatisms are due to an intrinsic cause (e.g. sleepwalking, brain tumours, epilepsy) and result in acquittal on the grounds of insanity. Sane automatisms are due to an extrinsic cause (e.g., confusional states, concussion, reflex actions after bee stings, dissociative states, sleep terrors, and hypoglycaemia) and result in complete acquittal.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 778.

Fire setting is the most common offense

stem: Which of the following is an actuarial tool for violence risk assessment?

It is reliant on historical factors and considered by some to be inflexible and unsuitable to inform risk management.

stem: Which of the following is true about sane automatism?
options: The defendant had control over their mind during the offence
Intent to harm need not be excluded
It is a very common defence in psychiatric patients
It results in complete acquittal if successful
correctAnswer: It results in complete acquittal if successful
explanation: If an individual commits an offence when their body is not under the control of their mind, (e.g. when asleep), they are not guilty of the offence. Legally, this is called an automatism. This defence has given rise to considerable problems, stemming mainly from the acquittal which results if it succeeds. As a result, courts have restricted the scope and availability of automatism, making it a rare plea. In England and Wales, two legal types of automatism are recognised: insane and sane (automatism simpliciter). The distinction is based on whether the behaviour is likely to recur. Insane automatisms are due to an intrinsic cause (e.g. sleepwalking, brain tumours, epilepsy) and result in acquittal on the grounds of insanity. Sane automatisms are due to an extrinsic cause (e.g., confusional states, concussion, reflex actions after bee stings, dissociative states, sleep terrors, and hypoglycaemia) and result in complete acquittal.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 778. Mackay RD. An anatomy of automatism. Medicine, Science and the Law. 2015 Jul;55(3):150-5.

stem: A 31-year-old man stalks his ex-wife with the hope that a reconciliation of their broken relationship will occur. He is most appropriately categorised as what type of stalker?
explanation: Typology of stalking perpetrators: · Rejected stalkers: pursue victims in order to reverse, correct, or avenge rejection (e.g. divorce, termination of relationship); previous sexual relationship; want to keep the victim in their lives · Intimacy seekers: infatuated with their victims and believe their victims are infatuated with them; no previous sexual relationship · Incompetent suitors: despite poor social or courting skills, have a fixation on (or in some cases a sense of entitlement to) an intimate relationship with those who have attracted their amorous interest · Resentful stalkers: pursue a vendetta because of a sense of grievance against the victim; motivated by a desire to frighten and distress; not following a sexual relationship · Predatory stalkers: initially spy on victims as a precursor to sexual assault; victim is often a stranger or acquaintance
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 742.

stem: A newly appointed executive of a forensic secure hospital board is exploring ways of improving the security of the units. Which of the following is best described as a measure of relational security?
options: Provision of meaningful activities to patients
Minimising the use of temporary members of staff
correctAnswer: Provision of meaningful activities to patients
explanation: Three concepts of security: 1. Physical/environmental – fence/locks and other means of securing against leaving the premises; also the use of soft cutlery, removing glasses, sharps and hanging points to reduce the risk of harm to self or others 2. Relational – training, good communication, meaningful activities, knowing patients well and developing good relationships with them; often a lack of relational security can decrease the actual safety net provided by the physical security measures 3. Procedural – searches, investigating and learning from incidents, staff pre-employment checks, other clinical governance arrangements, and risk management
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 750.

explanation: Stalking is a behaviour, not a mental disorder. Having said that, research suggests that 50% of stalking offenders have some sort of mental disorder. stem: Of those listed, what is the most common psychiatric diagnosis in perpetrators of arson?
explanation: Arson is a criminal act in which one willfully and maliciously sets fire to or aids in setting fire to a structure, dwelling, or property of another. Most arsonists are male, aged late adolescence-early adulthood, unmarried, poorly educated, living alone, and unemployed or unskilled labourers. Psychiatric disorders are over-represented in arsonists compared to the general population and other offender groups. Substance use disorders (especially alcohol) and personality disorders (particularly antisocial) are most common. Others include psychotic disorders and intellectual disability/low intellectual functioning.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 744. Burton P et al. Firesetting, arson, pyromania, and the forensic mental health expert. Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law Online. 2012 Sep 1;40(3):355-65.

correctAnswer: Psychoanalytic therapy is unlikely to be helpful
explanation: Treatments for fire setting are largely behavioural or focused on intervening in the family or intrapersonal stresses that may precipitate episodes of fire setting. Behavioural treatments like aversive therapy have helped fire setters (Koles and Jenson, 1985). Other treatment methods rely on positive reinforcement with threats of punishment and stimulus satiation. No established role has been shown for psychodynamic therapy.

stem: Which of the following terms used in medical jurisprudence refers to the (voluntary) act of crime?
explanation: According to criminal law, committing a socially harmful act is not the sole criterion of whether a crime has been committed. Instead, the objectionable act must have two components: actus reus and mens rea. Actus reus refers to the (voluntary) act of crime. Mens rea refers to the (evil) intent of crime. An evil intent cannot exist when an offender’s mental status is so deficient, so abnormal, or so diseased to have deprived the offender of the capacity for rational intent. Neither behaviour, however harmful, nor the intent to harm, alone, is grounds for criminal action.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 843.

stem: A married man was accused of indecent exposure and you have examined his mental state. You have to write a report. What will reduce his chance of re-offending?
explanation:
Court appearance and sentencing would sometimes reduce the risk of recidivism although this obviously depends on the offender's personality. Multiagency working (e.g. co-ordinated risk management MAPPA- probation, housing, social services, psychiatry etc.) and Sex Offender Treatment Programmes (SOTP) are the most important ways of reducing the risk of recidivism. Psychiatric treatment is unlikely to

be indicated in most sex offenders- including those convicted of indecent exposure. Polygraph assessment, psychosexual assessment, penile plethysmography are all helpful in risk assessment but not linked to reduction in recidivism, anti-androgens (this might reduce the risk of recidivism in serious sex offenders, but would obviously not be indicated for an offender whose offence is indecent exposure), SSRIs (these might be helpful for those who are depressed or obsessional, but only indicated in a small proportion).

stem: The MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool is most commonly used to evaluate which of the following?
explanation: In the United States, Hoge et al. developed and validated the MacArthur Structured Assessment of the Competence of Criminal Defendants to assess a defendant’s fitness to plead based on legal theory of competence. This 47-item measure was subsequently reduced to a 22-item clinical instrument, the MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool – Criminal Adjudication (MacCAT-CA). The MacCAT-CA was then modified to test abilities according to the criteria for fitness to stand trial in England and Wales. These changes include, for example, omitting reference to juries being involved in sentencing (a feature in some U.S. jurisdictions, but not in England and Wales) and adjusting offense designations. This process led to the development of a tool specific for England and Wales, the MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool – Fitness to Plead.
reference: Akinkunmi AA. The MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool--Fitness to plead: A preliminary evaluation of a research instrument for assessing fitness to plead in England and Wales. Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law. 2002.

stem: Pharmacotherapeutic options in the treatment of sex offenders include all of the following except
options: Combination of a GnRH agonist and SSRI
explanation: Since the 1990s, CBT has been the main modality of psychotherapeutic treatment for people convicted of sexual offences in the UK. Systematic use of medication only began to emerge in the early 2000s. The three classes of medications most often prescribed for problematic sexual behaviour include the SSRIs and two types of testosterone-lowering agents: the anti-androgens and the gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists. Treatment guidelines propose a hierarchical treatment protocol in which treatment is largely based on risk and progresses from psychotherapy (offered at all stages) to an ultimate stage where the combination of a GnRH agonist with an anti- androgen and/or SSRI is recommended. GnRH agonists are often considered preferable to anti-androgens whenever a testosterone- lowering medication is indicated as their side-effect profile appears to be relatively milder, and their effect more consistent.
reference: Winder B et al. The pharmacologic treatment of problematic sexual interests, paraphilic disorders, and sexual preoccupation in adult men who have committed a sexual offence. International Review of Psychiatry. 2019 Feb 17;31(2):159-68.

stem: Which of the following is most likely to be associated with amnesia for offending?
options: Psychotic symptoms at the time of the offence
Extreme emotional arousal during the offence
correctAnswer: Extreme emotional arousal during the offence
explanation: There may be three different explanations for memory loss in offenders. The first explanation contends that, during the time of the crime, some offenders suffer from a temporary (or permanent) brain dysfunction that prevents or undermines the storage of criminal events in memory (organic amnesia). The second explanation holds that some offenders are in an extreme emotional condition (e.g., rage) when committing a crime, particularly a violent crime. Later, the offender is unable to remember the crime because of a mismatch in emotional state between the encoding of crime-related events and the retrieval of such events (dissociative amnesia). The third explanation for crime- related amnesia is that a considerable number of offenders are pretending to be unable to remember crime-related details (feigned amnesia).
reference: Jelicic M. Testing claims of crime-related amnesia. Frontiers in Psychiatry. 2018 Nov 21;9:617.

stem: A 33-year-old man is charged with murder. His counsel pleads not guilty on the basis of sleepwalking. Sleepwalking may be accepted as an automatism provided that
options: The perpetrator has no previous history of sleepwalking
The perpetrator was able to narrate the event on waking up
The homicide took place within the first 2 hours of sleeping
The perpetrator has partial recall for the act
The perpetrator wakes up in the middle of the act with panic and screams
correctAnswer: The homicide took place within the first 2 hours of sleeping
explanation: If an individual commits an offence when their body is not under the control of their mind, (e.g. when asleep), they are not guilty of the offence. Legally, this is called an automatism. Insane automatisms are likely to recur and are due to an intrinsic cause (e.g. sleepwalking, brain tumours, epilepsy). Insane automatisms result in acquittal on the grounds of insanity. Sleepwalking involves complex, automatic behaviours (automatisms) such as wandering, attempting to dress or undress, carrying objects, eating, urinating in unusual places, and rarely driving a car or sexual behaviour. Behaviours usually occur 15-120 minutes following sleep onset. The activity never appears intentional or planned, and only rarely does aggressive behaviour occur. The person usually has no recollection of the episode. If awakened during the episode, they are usually confused and disoriented.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 460, 778.

stem: In forensic psychiatry, the Penrose hypothesis refers to which of the following?

The relationship between the prison population and psychiatric bed numbers

correctAnswer: The relationship between the prison population and psychiatric bed numbers
explanation: Penrose proposed an inverse relationship between the relative number of psychiatric beds available to a population and its total number of prisoners, based on calculations from cross-sectional study of 18 countries.
reference: Toynbee M. The Penrose hypothesis in the 21st century: revisiting the asylum. Evidence-based mental health. 2015 Aug 1;18(3):76.

stem: Which of the following is considered to be a test for fitness to give evidence in court?
options: Understanding the concept of criminal responsibility
Ability to understand questions posed by the court
correctAnswer: Ability to understand questions posed by the court
explanation: Though there is an absence of medical literature assessing the capacity to give evidence, legal competence in the UK requires that the person be able to understand questions and able to give answers that can be understood. Competence to give evidence is a decision for the judge, who may ask for the opinion of a psychiatrist or psychologist. The law presumes that ordinary individuals are competent and can be compelled to testify. Individuals may lack capacity to give evidence because of age or mental disorder.
reference: Jones R, Elliott T. Capacity to give evidence in court: issues that may arise when a client with dementia is a victim of crime. Psychiatric Bulletin. 2005 Sep;29(9):324-6.

stem:
Perpetrators of homicide For each of the following description choose the best term applicable from the list provided:

Killing of one's father Choose...

Killing of one's wife Choose...

Killing of one's child Choose...
correctAnswer: Killing of one's father → Patricide, Killing of one's wife → Uxoricide, Killing of one's child → Filicide
explanation: Explanation: Uxoricide (from Latin uxor meaning "wife") is the murder of one's wife. The act of murdering one's father is called patricide. Filicide is the deliberate act of a parent killing his or her son or daughter. The word filicide derives from the Latin words filius meaning "offspring".

Legal terminology (1) For each of the following description choose the best term applicable from the list below

The right to a hearing to determine if an accused is being legally detained before trial Choose...

An offence eligible for trial by the jury Choose...

The factual evidence for a crime to have been committed Choose...
correctAnswer: The right to a hearing to determine if an accused is being legally detained before trial → Habeas corpus, An offence eligible for trial by the jury → Indictable offence, The factual evidence for a crime to have been committed → Corpus deliciti
explanation:
Habeas corpus is Latin for "you may have the body" (subject to examination). It is a writ that requires a person detained by the authorities be brought before a court of law so that the legality of the detention could be examined. A summary offence are tried by a judge with no requirement for a jury at the trial hearing. An indictable offence, in contrast, is an offence that can only be tried after a preliminary hearing usually by the jury. In contrast to summary offences, indictable offenses are more serious

or complex in nature. (Ref: Retrieved from http://www.criminal-law-lawyer-source.com/terms/corpus-delicti.html) Corpus delicti is the legal term, which refers to the body of the offense or the essence of the crime. Most literally, corpus delicti is the term used to refer to the actual victim's body in a murder case. Corpus delicti is also a term that can be used to mean any material evidence of a crime or objective proof in a criminal case. The laws of corpus delicti relate to what must be proven in a case to elicit an acquittal or conviction.

Impulse control disorders Choose the most likely diagnosis from the following descriptions

A 34-year-old woman with failure to resist impulses to steal items that are not needed. Choose...

A 19-year-old man with mild learning difficulties has a history of multiple episodes of deliberate and purposeful fire setting Choose...

A 23-year-old woman with stereotyped recurrent pulling of hair, exacerbated by stress Choose...

A 64-year-old woman with persistent and recurrent maladaptive patterns of betting behaviour Choose...
correctAnswer:
A 34-year-old woman with failure to resist impulses to steal items that are not needed. → Kleptomania, A 19-year-old man with mild learning difficulties has a history of multiple episodes of deliberate and purposeful fire setting → Pyromania, A 23-year-old

woman with stereotyped recurrent pulling of hair, exacerbated by stress → Trichotillomania, A 64-year-old woman with persistent and recurrent maladaptive patterns of betting behaviour → Pathological gambling disorder
explanation: 1) Kleptomania is failure to resist impulses to steal items that are not needed or sought for personal use or monetary value. It is usually seen in females in their thirties. 2) Pyromania is the presence of multiple episodes of deliberate and purposeful fire setting leading to property damage, legal consequences and injury or loss of life. It is more prevalent in male adolescents with poor social skills and learning difficulties. 3) Trichotillomania is stereotyped recurrent pulling of hair, exacerbated by stress. Pulling hair relieves the feelings of tension, and it involves the scalp, eyelashes or eyebrows. 4) Pathological gambling disorder is persistent and recurrent maladaptive patterns of gambling behaviour. There is a preoccupation with gambling and needing to gamble with larger amounts of money to get the same feeling of excitement. It is relatively common and may lead to significant personal, family and occupational difficulties. (Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry- 386)

Forensic Psychiatry & Homicide Choose the most likely data pertaining to epidemiological observations for the following statements:

The proportion of homicide perpetrators with a primary diagnosis of a personality disorder that received prison sentence Choose...

What percentage of homicide perpetrators with a primary diagnosis of a personality disorder had no contact with the mental health services in the year before? Choose...

What percentage of PD patients had no other psychiatric illness at the time of committing the homicide? Choose...

What percentage of homicide perpetrators with a history of 'mental disorder' has personality disorders as a primary diagnosis? Choose...
correctAnswer: The proportion of homicide perpetrators with a primary diagnosis of a personality disorder that received prison sentence → 9%, What percentage of homicide perpetrators with a primary diagnosis of a personality disorder had no contact with the mental health services in the year before? → 7%, What percentage of PD patients had no other psychiatric illness at the time of committing the homicide? → 45%, What percentage of homicide perpetrators with a history of 'mental disorder' has personality disorders as a primary diagnosis? → 25-30%
explanation:
All of the required data to answer this EMI can be found in "Avoidable Deaths' - five-year report of the national confidential inquiry into

suicide and homicide by people with mental illness. www.nmhdu.org.uk/silo/files/avoidable-deaths-five-year-report-.pdf Among all homicide perpetrators, 30% have one or other mental disorder mentioned in the psychiatric reports, with around 10% having had a contact with mental health services in the last 12 months. Interestingly schizophrenia, alcohol /substance use and affective disorders are equally prevalent (18% each, of all those 30% with a 'diagnosis'), but the most common diagnosis is personality disorders (27%). In essence, 5% of all homicide perpetrators have a diagnosis of schizophrenia and another 5% have personality disorders as the primary diagnosis. Of the 5% perpetrators with a personality disorder, 29% had been in contact with services in the last 12 months, 28% had been in contact but not in the last 12 months and 43% had no previous contact with services at all. In total, 55% of the perpetrators with a PD had a secondary diagnosis, mainly alcohol and drug dependence. 92% of those with PD as a primary diagnosis are imprisoned, while 4 % receive hospital disposal. On the other hand, 29% of those with schizophrenia were imprisoned while 71% received a hospital order. In total, around 6% of homicide perpetrators receive a hospital disposal. Women and >65 age group are more likely to receive this outcome after a homicide. Among these, 70% have schizophrenia or related illnesses.

Measuring Tools in Forensic services For each of the following descriptions, identify the most appropriate tool from the list below;

Which of the listed tools is an outcome scale? Choose...

Which of the listed tools guide decisions regarding the need for secure placement Choose...

Which of the listed tools focuses on personality traits? Choose...
correctAnswer: Which of the listed tools is an outcome scale? → HoNOS-secure, Which of the listed tools guide decisions regarding the need for secure placement → DUNDRUM, Which of the listed tools focuses on personality traits? → HCL-R
explanation:
Sugarman & Walker adapted the HONOS scale by adding 'SECURE' items to enable its use in secure forensic settings. HONOS-Secure was previously known as HONOS-MDO. The 7 security rating items include risk of harm to adults or children; risk of self-harm (deliberate or accidental); need of building security to prevent physical escape; need for a safely staffed living environment; need for escort on leave (beyond the secure perimeter); risk to individual from others and the need for risk management procedures. HoNOS-secure is not a risk

assessment tool, but a tool that enable the clinical risk assessment to be translated to need for care and clinical risk management. DUNDRUM is a structure professional risk assessment tool to guide decisions regarding placement in forensic services. It defines eleven items relevant to the decision to allocate a person to high or medium security, low security, open hospital beds or community follow-up. HCL-R focuses on psychopathic traits
reference: http://www.rcpsych.ac.uk/quality/honos/secure.aspx Flynn, G., O'Neill, C., McInerney, C., & Kennedy, H. G. (2011). The DUNDRUM-1 structured professional judgment for triage to appropriate levels of therapeutic security: a retrospective cohort validation study. BMC Psychiatry, 11(1), 43.

stem:
Forensic epidemiology Using the most widely accepted epidemiological data, identify the probabilities associated with each of the following scenarios

The proportion of shoplifters that will reoffend after conviction Choose...

Proportion of prisoners that will self-harm during their prison term Choose...

The lifetime rate of any mental disorder in perpetrators of homicide Choose...

The probability of having a mental disorder at the time of committing a homicide offence Choose...
correctAnswer: The proportion of shoplifters that will reoffend after conviction → 10%, Proportion of prisoners that will self-harm during their prison term → 10%, The lifetime rate of any mental disorder in perpetrators of homicide → 30%, The probability of having a mental disorder at the time of committing a homicide offence → 10%
explanation:
Around 90% of shoplifters, when convicted, will not reoffend. The remaining 10% will repeat the offence. Self-harm is much more prevalent among prisoners than among the general population. One-half of female remand prisoners have self-

harmed at some time in their lives and more than one-quarter in the previous year. The corresponding figures for men are about half of these. Perhaps as many as 10% of prisoners will self-harm during their term with the likelihood increasing with the length of time in custody. Highest rates are among sentenced female prisoners who have spent two or more years in prison, 23% of whom will have self-harmed during the current term (Meltzer et al., 1999). A national clinical survey of people convicted of homicide (n=1594) in England and Wales (1996-1999) showed that (34%) had a mental disorder: most had not attended psychiatric services; 85 (5%) had schizophrenia (lifetime); 164 (10%) had symptoms of mental illness at the time of the offence; 149 (9%) received a diminished responsibility verdict and 111 (7%) a hospital disposal - both were associated with severe mental illness and symptoms of psychosis.
reference: Ihttp://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK56398/ Shaw, J., Hunt, I. M., Flynn, S., Meehan, J., Robinson, J. O., Bickley, H., ... & Appleby, L. (2006). Rates of mental disorder in people convicted of homicide. The British Journal of Psychiatry, 188(2), 143-147.
